title: Amazon S3 Video Storage
content:
Step 1: Create the Video Bucket Go to Amazon S3 > Create bucket. Bucket type: General purpose > Bucket name: securelearn-media-<account-id>. Block all public access: keep it on. There is no public URL like pub-*.r2.dev any more; videos are only reachable through presigned URLs signed by the backend. Default encryption: choose SSE-KMS > key SecureLearn-Key (section 5.3.4) > Bucket Key: Enable. Click Create bucket. The active backend workflow uses these prefixes:
videos/{courseId}/: raw videos uploaded by instructors, deleted by the backend after processing. hls/{courseId}/{lesson-name}/: master.m3u8, content.key (16-byte AES-128 key) and each lesson’s encrypted segment_XXX.ts files. models/: the AI Lambda’s model.pkl. The optional MediaConvert exercise in section 5.4.4 writes HLS without AES-128 media encryption to mediaconvert-output/{courseId}/{lesson-name}/. S3 still applies the bucket’s default SSE-KMS encryption at rest. This separate prefix is not used by the current playback backend.
Step 2: Configure CORS The browser PUTs the raw video (15-minute presigned URL) and downloads segments after the backend’s 302 (60-second presigned URL) directly from S3, so the bucket must allow CORS.
Permissions tab > Cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) > Edit, paste: [ { "AllowedOrigins": ["https://learn.yourdomain.com", "http://localhost:3000"], "AllowedMethods": ["GET", "HEAD", "PUT"], "AllowedHeaders": ["*"], "ExposeHeaders": ["ETag"], "MaxAgeSeconds": 3000 } ] Click Save changes. Step 3: Create a Lifecycle Rule (recommended) Management tab > Create lifecycle rule > Name: cleanup-source-videos. Prefix: videos/ > check Expire current versions of objects > Days: 1. Click Create rule (removes raw videos left behind by failed processing). Step 4: Test the Pipeline After finishing section 5.4.2, sign in as an INSTRUCTOR, upload a short video (under 1 minute), then check:
aws s3 ls s3://securelearn-media-<account-id>/hls/ --recursive | head aws s3 cp s3://securelearn-media-<account-id>/hls/<courseId>/<tên-bài>/master.m3u8 - | head -8 The playlist must contain #EXT-X-KEY:METHOD=AES-128,URI="securelearn-key", and videos/ no longer holds the raw video. Opening a segment’s S3 URL without a signature returns 403 AccessDenied.

title: Workshop Overview
content:
1. Problem Statement & Solution Overview Small and medium-sized educational centers (SMEs) face severe intellectual property leakage when lecture videos are downloaded, screen-recorded, and redistributed illegally. Commercial DRM solutions (Widevine, PlayReady) carry prohibitive licensing fees and integration complexity.
SecureLearn is an LMS with a ReactJS frontend and a Spring Boot backend that protects videos in several layers:
Media Pipeline: Instructors upload source videos directly to Amazon S3 using presigned URLs. The Spring Boot backend on Amazon ECS Fargate uses MediaConvert to convert them to HLS (6-second segments) and encrypts every segment with AES-128 using a per-lesson key. Delivery & Access Control: Students authenticate via Amazon Cognito (JWT). The backend issues a playback token (HMAC-SHA256, 2-hour TTL), only returns the decryption key to the token holder, and serves each segment through a 60-second S3 presigned URL. The ReactJS frontend is delivered through Amazon CloudFront (filtered by AWS WAF), and business data lives in Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. Security & Key Management: AWS KMS and AWS Secrets Manager protect API credentials, while AWS CloudTrail logs all audit events. AI & Leak Tracing: AWS EventBridge triggers an Isolation Forest Lambda function every 5 minutes to detect abnormal access patterns and send alerts via Amazon SNS, paired with a JavaScript dynamic watermark displaying the student’s User ID and IP. 2. AMAZON LINUX AMI VS. WINDOWS AMI: WHICH IS THE BETTER CHOICE WHEN CREATING AN EC2 INSTANCE? When creating an EC2 instance on AWS, choosing between Amazon Linux 2023 and Windows Server AMI involves trade-offs regarding usability, system resources, and operating costs.
Key points to know: Windows AMI – Accessible but High Cost: Features a familiar Graphical User Interface (GUI) and management via Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP), making it very friendly for beginners. However, it requires substantial hardware resources (at least 2 GB of RAM; t3.micro/nano are discouraged) and includes additional operating system licensing fees. Amazon Linux 2023 – Optimized Performance and Cost: Built specifically for cloud and enterprise applications focusing on security, high stability, and no separate operating system fees. SSH management is lightweight, highly resource-efficient, and does not require desktop interface maintenance. The Linux Learning Curve: Linux requires users to master the command line, file management, and permissions, and may necessitate supplementary tools like MobaXterm, Git, or remote development environments for smooth workflows. Decision Guide: If an application strictly requires Microsoft technologies (such as legacy .NET Framework or IIS), Windows is the definitive choice. Otherwise, for general workloads like web servers, APIs, and Node.js, Amazon Linux 2023 is the preferred choice due to superior cost optimization and long-term automation capabilities. title: Blog 2
content:
CENTRALIZED MANAGEMENT OF HUNDREDS OF AWS ACCOUNTS SECURELY WITH ORGANIZATIONS & SERVICE CONTROL POLICIES (SCPs) Managing systems under a single AWS Account model poses significant risks of information security breaches and service disruptions as scale grows or when applying automated tools such as AI Agents. To completely resolve this challenge, AWS recommends adopting a Multi-Account strategy combined with AWS Organizations and Service Control Policies (SCPs).
Key points to know: Single-Account Model Risks & Challenges from AI Agents: Consolidating all environments (Dev, Staging, Prod) into a single account easily leads to a complete system crash when an incident occurs. Additionally, operating automated AI Agents without organization-level guardrails can lead to manipulation (Prompt Injection), resulting in wasted costs or accidental deletion of critical resources. AWS Standard Multi-Account Architecture: Clearly separate the Management Account (root account used solely for management/billing), Organizational Units - OUs (such as Security OU, Workload OU), and enforce centralized security boundaries. The Role of Service Control Policies (SCPs): SCPs establish maximum privilege limits applied across individual OUs or member accounts. SCPs help protect audit data (blocking deletion/disabling of CloudTrail), restrict geographic regions (limiting resource provisioning to approved regions only), lock down sensitive resources (S3, RDS), and prevent member accounts from leaving the organization autonomously. Centralized Monitoring: Combine automated log collection via AWS CloudTrail Organizational Trails, configuration management using AWS Config Aggregator, and automated activation of AWS GuardDuty for all newly created accounts. 3-Step Migration Roadmap: (1) Initialize AWS Organizations & centralized SSO login -> (2) Plan OU structures & separate environments -> (3) Tighten SCPs & automate account provisioning using AWS Control Tower. Reference [1] AWS Documentation - Service Control Policies (SCPs) (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps.html) [2] AWS Documentation - Example Service Control Policies (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps_examples.html) [3] AWS Builder Center - Protecting AWS Organization with SCPs (https://builder.aws.com/content/3ItkGyU0Nn5rfYhYQOkbvFiUQ2O/introduction-to-aws-organizations-and-service-control-policies-scps)

title: Blog 1
content:
AWS Security: Zero Trust & Least Privilege In many traditional network systems, security is often established based on network boundaries. This means that if you are inside the internal network, you are trusted by default. While this approach is quite simple, it is no longer secure enough in a modern cloud environment. If an attacker manages to bypass the outer perimeter, the system can be fully compromised due to the lack of strict protection layers inside. While exploring AWS, I came across some interesting documents regarding the implementation of Zero Trust architecture and the principle of Least Privilege. These articles (including one from AWS Builder Center published in September 2026) dive deep into how to shift from network-based trust to identity-based trust. What I found particularly fascinating is that solving this challenge does not rely on a single service; rather, it combines multiple AWS services into a complete, multi-layered defense system.
THE PROBLEM TO BE SOLVED Imagine a cloud system where services and users constantly interact with one another:
Users accessing internal applications. Microservices connecting to databases. Third-party applications invoking internal APIs. Management devices connecting to servers. If we rely solely on network locations—such as assuming “Any request coming from a Private Subnet is safe by default”—the system could face immense risks. In this scenario, granting permissions based on network location is no longer trustworthy. The solution introduced by AWS is building a Zero Trust security model—never trust anyone or any system by default, regardless of where they are located. AWS ARCHITECTURE AND CORE PRINCIPLES One of the aspects I really like about the Zero Trust model on AWS is how the system divides the defense pipeline into multiple components based on strict principles:
Verify and Authenticate: AWS requires every user and system to continuously prove their identity on a per-request basis rather than logging in just once. The system evaluates context data points such as user identity, location, and device health to grant access. Least Privilege Access: Users or services are granted only the minimum permissions necessary to perform their tasks. AWS IAM Access Analyzer is used to detect over-privileged permissions and refine exact boundaries. Micro-segmentation: Data and systems are divided into small, strictly isolated segments. AWS Transit Gateway and Security Groups are used to isolate sensitive workloads within Amazon VPC. Automation & Monitoring: The system is continuously monitored to detect risks and trigger alerts. AWS GuardDuty and AWS Security Hub continuously analyze events to automatically detect threats or anomalous behaviors. HOW DOES ZERO TRUST WORK? Not all access requests are allowed through easily just because they originate within an internal network. Under this model, the system applies the “Assume Breach” principle—always assuming that the system may already be compromised and restricting all possible attack paths. For example, instead of just checking an IP address like a traditional network:10.0.0.123 The system performs a comprehensive evaluation of the context: Identity: Role App-Backend Action: s3:GetObject Resource: arn:aws:s3:::customer-data Condition: MFA Active = True, Source VPC = vpc-12345 Based on this contextual identity information, the system makes an access decision, even if the IP address belongs to a trusted zone. This is a critical distinction: protection is identity-driven rather than reliant solely on a simple network perimeter. Data encryption and network controls are also strictly enforced to minimize blast radiuses.
KEY TAKEAWAYS The most notable realization after reading these documents is the perspective that Zero Trust is not a off-the-shelf product you can just buy.More importantly, Zero Trust is an architectural mindset that must be deeply engineered into the cloud system. AWS IAM handles core identity management, while other services take responsibility for network segmentation, traffic control, monitoring, and automated incident response.You can visualize a basic workflow as follows:Authentication via IAM → Network Traffic Control via Security Groups/VPC → Event Monitoring via CloudTrail → Threat Analysis & Detection via GuardDuty.Each service addresses a specific problem, but when combined, they form a robust defense in depth mechanism that cannot be easily broken.Through this, I also realized that when building real-world cloud applications, getting code to run successfully is only a small part of the job. The security architecture surrounding those cloud resources plays a vital role in survival.
CONCLUSION The documents on Zero Trust and Least Privilege offered me a very insightful perspective on re-architecting security on AWS. Instead of building a large external firewall and letting everything inside communicate freely, AWS guides us on how to continuously verify and minimize access privileges for every single service. In particular, combining Identity Management and Networking completely eliminates the biggest weaknesses of traditional security models. In my opinion, this is a essential mindset to explore for anyone learning AWS or DevOps who wants to apply security principles directly into real-world enterprise scenarios.
References [1] AWS Security - Zero Trust on AWS: https://aws.amazon.com/security/zero-trust/[cite: 1] [2] Zero Trust Security in AWS: Protecting Modern Cloud Infrastructure: https://builder.aws.com/content/3J2jVMOX6TBxqaso1EDDmXZxa8S/zero-trust-security-in-aws-protecting-modern-cloud-infrastructure[cite: 1] [3] Understanding Zero Trust principles - AWS Prescriptive Guidance: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/strategy-zero-trust-architecture/zero-trust-principles.html[cite: 1] Link blog: https://www.facebook.com/groups/660548818043427/user/100053180442383

title: AI Anomaly Detection Lambda
content:
Step 1: Create Lambda AnomalyDetection Go to AWS Lambda > Create event function. Select Author from scratch > Function name: SecureLearn-AnomalyDetection `
Runtime: Select Node.js 20.x / Python 3.12. Custom settings / Additional settings: Leave as default
Click Create function. Code to load an AI model, read logs (simulated), detect anomalies, and send alerts via SNS. (The Isolation Forest model (.pkl file) and libraries such as scikit-learn, numpy, and scipy must be packaged into a Lambda Layer—installed within the python/lib/python3.12/site-packages/ directory and compressed as a ZIP file.)
import os, json, pickle, datetime as dt from collections import defaultdict import boto3 from boto3.dynamodb.conditions import Key TABLE = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table(os.environ["TABLE_NAME"]) S3 = boto3.client("s3") SNS = boto3.client("sns") WINDOW_MINUTES = 5 _model = None def load_model(): # 1. Tải model.pkl từ S3 (giữ trong bộ nhớ giữa các lần gọi) global _model if _model is None: obj = S3.get_object(Bucket=os.environ["MODEL_BUCKET"], Key=os.environ["MODEL_KEY"]) _model = pickle.loads(obj["Body"].read()) return _model def fetch_logs(): # 2. Query GSI LogInADay lấy log 5 phút gần nhất (query cả 2 ngày nếu vắt qua nửa đêm) now = dt.datetime.now(dt.timezone.utc) start = now - dt.timedelta(minutes=WINDOW_MINUTES) items = [] for day in sorted({start.strftime("%Y-%m-%d"), now.strftime("%Y-%m-%d")}): kwargs = { "IndexName": os.environ["GSI_NAME"], "KeyConditionExpression": Key("day").eq(day) & Key("timestamp").between(start.isoformat(), now.isoformat()), } while True: resp = TABLE.query(**kwargs) items.extend(resp["Items"]) if "LastEvaluatedKey" not in resp: break kwargs["ExclusiveStartKey"] = resp["LastEvaluatedKey"] return items def build_features(items): # 3. Đặc trưng theo từng tài khoản (thứ tự phải giống lúc huấn luyện): # [số request, số IP, số thiết bị, số bài học, số request KEY] acc = defaultdict(lambda: {"n": 0, "ips": set(), "fps": set(), "lessons": set(), "keys": 0}) for it in items: a = acc[it["username"]] a["n"] += 1 a["ips"].add(it.get("ip")) a["fps"].add(it.get("fingerprint")) a["lessons"].add(it.get("lessonId")) if it.get("action") == "KEY": a["keys"] += 1 users = list(acc) X = [[acc[u]["n"], len(acc[u]["ips"]), len(acc[u]["fps"]), len(acc[u]["lessons"]), acc[u]["keys"]] for u in users] return users, X def lambda_handler(event, context): items = fetch_logs() if not items: return {"scanned": 0, "flagged": 0} users, X = build_features(items) preds = load_model().predict(X) # -1 = bất thường, 1 = bình thường flagged = [ {"username": u, "requests": x[0], "distinct_ips": x[1], "distinct_devices": x[2], "distinct_lessons": x[3], "key_requests": x[4]} for u, x, p in zip(users, X, preds) if p == -1 ] # 4. Nếu phát hiện bất thường, gửi cảnh báo qua SNS if flagged: SNS.publish( TopicArn=os.environ["SNS_TOPIC_ARN"], Subject="[SecureLearn] AI Anomaly Alert", Message=json.dumps(flagged, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2), ) return {"scanned": len(users), "flagged": len(flagged)} Click Deploy.
Configure environment variables: Go to Configuration > Environment variables > Edit, and add the following two variables: GSI_NAME: LogInADay MODEL_BUCKET: securelearn-media- (tạo ở mục 5.4.1). MODEL_KEY: models/model.pkl SNS_TOPIC_ARN: ARN của SNS Topic SecureLearn-Alerts (sẽ tạo ở mục 5.3.5).
Vào Configuration > General configuration > Edit: Memory 1024 MB, Timeout 1 min.

title: Spring Boot Backend on ECS
content:
The Spring Boot backend serves the whole /api/v1/* API and runs on ECS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer. Spring Boot handles routing, validates Cognito JWTs (oauth2ResourceServer), and authorizes by group.
Step 1: Create the VPC & Security Groups Go to VPC (region ap-southeast-1) > Create VPC > select VPC and more. Name tag: securelearn > IPv4 CIDR: 10.0.0.0/16 > Number of AZs: 2 > Public subnets: 2 > Private subnets: 2 > NAT gateways: None > VPC endpoints: S3 Gateway > Click Create VPC. Go to Security groups > Create security group (VPC securelearn-vpc) and create 3 groups: securelearn-alb-sg: inbound HTTPS 443 from prefix list com.amazonaws.global.cloudfront.origin-facing (only CloudFront can reach the ALB). securelearn-ecs-sg: inbound TCP 8080 from securelearn-alb-sg. securelearn-rds-sg: inbound PostgreSQL 5432 from securelearn-ecs-sg. ECS Fargate, the ALB and RDS must live in a VPC. The security-group chain above ensures Internet → only CloudFront reaches the ALB → only the ALB reaches the container → only the container reaches the database. No NAT Gateway is created to save cost; the ECS task runs in a public subnet with a public IP.
Step 2: Create RDS for PostgreSQL Go to RDS > Subnet groups > Create DB subnet group > Name: securelearn-db-subnets > select the 2 private subnets > Create. Databases > Create database > Standard create > Engine: PostgreSQL 16 > Templates: Free tier. DB instance identifier: securelearn-db > Master username: securelearn > Credentials management: Self managed, set a password (stored in Secrets Manager in section 5.3.4). Instance class: db.t4g.micro > Storage: gp3 20 GiB. Connectivity: VPC securelearn-vpc > subnet group securelearn-db-subnets > Public access: No > Security group: securelearn-rds-sg. Additional configuration > Initial database name: securelearn > Click Create database and note the Endpoint. The backend runs with spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update, so Hibernate creates the Course, Chapter, Lesson tables on first start.
Step 3: Build & Push the Image to Amazon ECR Check that the Dockerfile installs ffmpeg (image eclipse-temurin:25-jre), then create the repository and push the image (run in backend/):
ACCOUNT_ID=<account-id> REGION=ap-southeast-1 REGISTRY=$ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.$REGION.amazonaws.com aws ecr create-repository --repository-name securelearn-backend --region $REGION aws ecr get-login-password --region $REGION | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin $REGISTRY docker build --platform linux/amd64 -t $REGISTRY/securelearn-backend:v1 . docker push $REGISTRY/securelearn-backend:v1 Step 4: Create IAM Roles for ECS Go to IAM > Roles > Create role > AWS service > Elastic Container Service Task and create 2 roles:
securelearn-ecs-execution-role: attach AmazonECSTaskExecutionRolePolicy and an inline policy allowing secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on the securelearn/backend secret and kms:Decrypt on the SecureLearn-Key key (section 5.3.4). securelearn-ecs-task-role: inline policy for the backend code (replacing the R2/AWS access keys): { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject", "s3:DeleteObject"], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::securelearn-media-<account-id>/*" }, { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["kms:Decrypt", "kms:GenerateDataKey"], "Resource": "<kms-key-arn>" }, { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["dynamodb:PutItem", "dynamodb:GetItem", "dynamodb:Query"], "Resource": ["arn:aws:dynamodb:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:table/AccessLog", "arn:aws:dynamodb:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:table/AccessLog/index/*"] }, { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["cognito-idp:AdminCreateUser", "cognito-idp:AdminDeleteUser", "cognito-idp:AdminGetUser", "cognito-idp:AdminAddUserToGroup", "cognito-idp:AdminListGroupsForUser", "cognito-idp:AdminSetUserPassword", "cognito-idp:ListUsers", "cognito-idp:ListUsersInGroup"], "Resource": "arn:aws:cognito-idp:ap-southeast-1:<account-id>:userpool/<user-pool-id>" } ] } Step 5: Create the Application Load Balancer Go to Certificate Manager (region ap-southeast-1) > Request > domain *.yourdomain.com (wildcard, covering both origin and learn because CloudFront forwards the viewer’s Host header) > DNS validation > Create records in Route 53. EC2 > Target groups > Create target group > Target type: IP > Name: securelearn-backend-tg > HTTP port 8080 > VPC securelearn-vpc > Health check path: /api/v1/allcourses (public endpoint; the backend has no Actuator) > Create (register no targets). Load balancers > Create > Application Load Balancer > Name: securelearn-alb > Internet-facing > the 2 public subnets > security group securelearn-alb-sg > Listener: HTTPS 443 forwarding to securelearn-backend-tg with the new certificate > Create. Attributes tab > Idle timeout: 300 seconds (for long upload/processing requests). Generate a secret with openssl rand -hex 32. Open the HTTPS:443 listener: Default action: Return fixed response 403. Add rule: condition HTTP header X-Origin-Verify = the secret > forward to securelearn-backend-tg. Route 53 > create record origin.yourdomain.com (A, Alias) pointing to securelearn-alb. Step 6: Create the Task Definition & ECS Service Do this step after creating the secret in section 5.3.4.
Go to ECS > Task definitions > Create new task definition: Family: securelearn-backend > Launch type: AWS Fargate > CPU 2 vCPU / Memory 4 GB > Ephemeral storage: 50 GiB (room for FFmpeg’s raw video and temp segments). Task execution role: securelearn-ecs-execution-role; Task role: securelearn-ecs-task-role. Container: name backend, image <account-id>.dkr.ecr.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com/securelearn-backend:v1, port 8080. Environment variables (matching application.properties from Step 3): AWS_REGION = ap-southeast-1 SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL = jdbc:postgresql://<rds-endpoint>:5432/securelearn SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME = securelearn S3_BUCKET_NAME = securelearn-media-<account-id> COGNITO_POOL_ID, COGNITO_CLIENT_ID = values from section 5.3.1 CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS = https://learn.yourdomain.com LEGACY_PUBLIC_BASE_URL = the old https://pub-xxxx.r2.dev URL (only needed while migrating data, see section 5.4.1) JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS = -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=60 Secrets (ValueFrom): SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD = <secret-arn>:SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD::, COGNITO_CLIENT_SECRET = <secret-arn>:COGNITO_CLIENT_SECRET::, PLAYBACK_TOKEN_SECRET = <secret-arn>:PLAYBACK_TOKEN_SECRET::. Log collection: Amazon CloudWatch > Click Create. Clusters > Create cluster > Name: securelearn-cluster > AWS Fargate > Create. Open the cluster > Services > Create: Launch type: FARGATE > Task definition: securelearn-backend > Service name: securelearn-backend-svc > Desired tasks: 1. Networking: VPC securelearn-vpc > the 2 public subnets > security group securelearn-ecs-sg > Public IP: On. Load balancing: use the existing securelearn-alb > listener 443:HTTPS > target group securelearn-backend-tg > Health check grace period: 180 seconds. Click Create, wait for the task to be RUNNING and the target group to report healthy. The Started SecureLearnApplication log line in CloudWatch means the backend reached RDS and Cognito. Main Backend APIs POST /api/v1/auth/register, /otp, /login, /refresh, /forgot-password, /reset-password: sign-up, OTP confirmation, sign-in through Cognito (USER_PASSWORD_AUTH + SECRET_HASH). GET /api/v1/lesson/{id}/playback: issue an HMAC playback token (2-hour TTL). GET .../manifest, .../key, .../segment/{n}: return the rewritten manifest, the AES-128 key, and a 302 redirect to a 60-second S3 presigned URL. POST /api/v1/upload/presign, /api/v1/upload/process (INSTRUCTOR/ADMIN): request an upload URL (15-minute TTL) and ask FFmpeg to process the video. /api/v1/admin/*: user management (ADMIN only once authorization is fixed, see section 5.4.3). The optional MediaConvert job in section 5.4.4 is a separate test flow. The current upload endpoint does not submit MediaConvert jobs; keep its output in mediaconvert-output/ and do not overwrite the encrypted hls/ files.
/upload/process currently runs synchronously, and CloudFront waits at most 60 seconds, so long videos report a timeout even though the backend finishes processing. Use short videos for demos, or change the code to return 202 and process in the background.

title: Event 2
content:
Summary Report: “AWS CLOUD AND AI DAY HANOI” Event Objectives The “AWS Cloud and AI Day Hanoi” event was organized to provide a direct networking space between the Vietnamese technology community and leading experts from AWS and enterprise partners. The event focuses on the following strategic objectives:
Update pioneering technology trends: Introduce cloud solutions, modern data architectures, and especially the explosion of Agentic AI and Generative AI in optimizing operational processes. Hands-on practice and real-world experience: Provide a practical environment through hands-on workshops, helping developers and engineers directly build and deploy AI Agent solutions right at the event. Community and enterprise networking: Create a launching pad for exchanges and experience sharing among IT managers, solution architects, and leading technology experts. Speakers The event brought together a team of speakers representing regulatory agencies, technology corporation leaders, and solution experts from AWS:
Phạm Đức Long – Deputy Minister of Information and Communications / Ministry of Science & Technology Jennifer Wicks – U.S. Ambassador to Vietnam Dr. Werner Vogels – Chief Technology Officer (CTO), Amazon.com Eric Yeo – Country General Manager (Malaysia, Vietnam, Indochina), AWS Dr. Jens Lottner – Chief Executive Officer (CEO), Techcombank Mai Le – Director of Product Management, Katalon Along with top Solutions Architects and Engineers from AWS and partners VPBank, Cloud Kinetics. Key Highlights The program took place with more than 30 in-depth sharing sessions, covering key topics:
Keynote: Breaking limits with Agentic AI and AWS The opening session focused on the question “What if we turn every idea into reality?”. Speakers reviewed how AWS equips tools for modern builders, while listening to success stories from Techcombank and Katalon when bringing AI into their operational core.
Transformation and System Modernization with Agentic AI: Technical sessions went deep into applying AI Agents to solve legacy application modernization problems and accelerate the software development process: Migration at Scale with AWS Transform: Methods for modernizing large applications and infrastructure, reducing technical debt through automated agents. Building next-generation applications: Leveraging Agentic AI to automate the SDLC cycle from planning, coding to maintenance. AI-Ready Data Foundation To run AI models effectively, data plays a decisive prerequisite role. The discussion session focused on standardizing data architecture, large-scale data processing workflows, and security to ensure accuracy for AI applications.
Key Takeaways Attending the event helped accumulate many new perspectives from both mindset and practical deployment techniques.
Architectural & Strategic Mindset Agentic AI Shift: Clearly recognized the shift from pure Generative AI (generating content) to Agentic AI (having the capability to self-plan, make decisions, and execute tasks). Data-First Mindset: To successfully deploy AI in enterprises, the foundational factor does not lie in the model but in the structure and quality of underlying data. In-depth Techniques: Understood the application modernization process using AWS automation tools, helping shorten system conversion time. Grasped how to set up an Internal Developer Platform (IDP) on EKS to accelerate software delivery speed. Skills to integrate large language models (LLMs) into workflows through the AWS service ecosystem. Applying to Work The knowledge acquired from the event brings clear application value to current and future projects:
Application to Projects & Major Assignments: Experiment with integrating AI services like Amazon Bedrock/Amazon Q into student software projects to optimize development processes. Cloud & AI Learning Orientation: Supplement knowledge of Microservices, Serverless, and Kubernetes (EKS) architectures on the AWS platform into the self-study roadmap. Internship Preparation: Leverage knowledge about Agentic AI and Cloud to enrich the capability profile (CV), preparing for upcoming internship opportunities. Event Experience The “AWS Cloud and AI Day Hanoi” event was a learning journey that brought many emotional and practical values. Not stopping at theoretical presentations, the event brought an energetic innovative atmosphere.
Impressions on Scale and Speakers The presence of big names like CTO Werner Vogels along with representatives from Ministries and large banks affirmed the importance of the Cloud/AI technology wave in Vietnam. How speakers conveyed real business problems made the technology picture extremely close and rich in strategic value.
Impressions on Professional Content and AI Trends Technical sharing sessions were designed from basic to advanced levels, very suitable for students to follow and take notes.
Approaching Agentic AI trends: Through presentations like “Building software like never before with agentic AI”, I visualized more clearly how programmers will work in the near future when combining with AI Agents. Time Saving & Proactive Absorption: Participating remotely helped me flexibly choose to follow sharing sessions most suitable for my personal learning orientation. Watch Party & Interactive Environment At the online connection point in Ho Chi Minh City, I still felt the heat from the main event in Hanoi.
Discussing with friends: Exchanging and discussing demonstrated solutions with fellow students and the AWS community in Ho Chi Minh City. Inspiring learning: The event helped me realize the importance of proactively learning new technologies like Cloud & AI right while sitting in school chairs to avoid falling behind. Summary: The event not only brought an updated volume of technical knowledge but also strongly inspired innovative thinking, helping me become more confident in proposing and deploying modern AI & Cloud solutions into practical work. Some event photos Overall, the event not only provided technical knowledge but also helped me reshape my thinking about application design, system modernization, and cross-team collaboration.

title: Proposal
content:
SecureLearn: Digital Content Protection System for Educational Platforms — AWS Well-Architected Standards Digital Content Protection System for Educational Platforms — AWS Well-Architected Standards 1. Executive Summary SecureLearn is a low-cost video content protection solution for small and medium-sized training centers (SMEs) that runs entirely on AWS.
A Spring Boot backend on Amazon ECS Fargate handles authentication (Amazon Cognito), authorization, video processing and business logic. The ReactJS frontend is delivered through Amazon S3 + Amazon CloudFront and protected by AWS WAF. Videos are converted to HLS and encrypted with AES-128 by MediaConvert. Viewing rights are controlled by JWTs and short-lived playback tokens, and each segment can only be downloaded through a 60-second presigned URL. The system combines behavioral AI (Isolation Forest on AWS Lambda) with dynamic watermarking to protect intellectual property. 2. Problem Statement What’s the Problem? In the era of digital education, small and medium-sized training centers (SMEs) and e-learning platforms face serious intellectual-property loss as lecture videos are downloaded, screen-recorded and redistributed without permission on social networks. Large-scale commercial DRM solutions (such as Google Widevine and Microsoft PlayReady) carry very high licensing costs and integration complexity, beyond the budget of most SMEs.
The Solution SecureLearn uses a serverless container architecture on AWS:
Video processing: The Spring Boot backend on Amazon ECS Fargate generates an AES-128 key unique to the lesson and creates an AWS Elemental MediaConvert job. MediaConvert converts the video to HLS and encrypts every segment with AES-128 using the lesson’s key, writing the output to S3. Data: course data lives in Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, access logs in Amazon DynamoDB, and videos in private Amazon S3. Delivery: Amazon CloudFront, AWS WAF and an Application Load Balancer deliver the frontend and API securely. Core features: JWT authentication through Amazon Cognito, short-lived HMAC playback tokens, AI anomaly detection with Isolation Forest on Lambda and EventBridge, dynamic watermarking and automatic alerts through Amazon SNS. Comparative Table of Current Issues, Business Impacts, and AWS Solutions:
Current Issue Business Impact SecureLearn Solution (AWS / Cloudflare) Videos downloaded & illegally shared Revenue loss, leakage of exclusive lecture IP AES-128 encrypted HLS produced by MediaConvert; the decryption key is only returned to holders of a valid playback token; segments are only downloadable through 60-second S3 presigned URLs Lack of proactive monitoring Failure to detect account sharing or video crawling in real-time Every playback request is logged to DynamoDB (IP, device fingerprint); an Isolation Forest Lambda scans logs every 5 minutes and alerts through SNS Inability to trace leaks Unable to identify culprits when videos are screen-recorded A dynamic watermark shows the learner ID and time, moving continuously over the video player High commercial DRM costs SMEs cannot afford infrastructure upkeep AWS managed services (ECS Fargate, RDS, S3, CloudFront), no server administration, no DRM licensing fees; AWS Free Tier credits cover the early phase Benefits and Return on Investment The solution needs no physical or virtual server administration and no commercial DRM licensing. It protects exclusive content, prevents unauthorized account sharing, monitors anomalies automatically and supports leak tracing. Estimated infrastructure cost is about $165 USD/month running 24/7 (about $60–75 USD/month when only running during working hours).
3. Solution Architecture The system runs entirely on AWS, with no traditional server administration, and is organized into 4 functional layers:
Media Pipeline (Upload & Processing): Instructors request a presigned URL from the backend and upload the raw video straight to Amazon S3 (SSE-KMS encryption at rest). The Spring Boot backend on ECS Fargate downloads the raw video and uses MediaConvert to transcode it to HLS (6-second segments, H.264/AAC), encrypting it with AES-128 using a per-lesson key. The backend stores segment_XXX.ts, content.key and master.m3u8 in S3, writes the lesson to RDS PostgreSQL and deletes the raw video. Delivery & Access Control: Learners sign in through Amazon Cognito and receive a JWT. The backend validates the JWT, issues an HMAC-SHA256 playback token (2-hour lifetime) and rewrites the manifest so both the key and the segments must go through the backend. The AES-128 key is only returned to the token holder. Each segment is redirected (302) to a 60-second S3 presigned URL. The ReactJS frontend is served from S3 through CloudFront; /api/* goes through CloudFront → ALB → ECS. Security & Key Management: AWS WAF filters requests at CloudFront: managed rules, rate limiting and an IP allow-list for admin APIs. AWS KMS and AWS Secrets Manager protect the database password, the Cognito client secret and the token-signing key. The backend uses an IAM role instead of access keys. Security groups only allow the CloudFront → ALB → ECS → RDS chain. AWS CloudTrail records audit logs. AI & Tracing: Offline training using Isolation Forest in Jupyter Notebooks (.pkl model stored in R2); AWS Lambda (triggered by EventBridge every 5 mins) reads access logs from DynamoDB/CloudWatch, runs anomaly inference, and publishes alerts via Amazon SNS; JavaScript-based dynamic watermarks display moving user IDs. Data Flow Diagrams:
Upload flow: Instructor → CloudFront → ALB → ECS (request presigned URL) → Browser PUTs the video to S3 videos/ → ECS ( create key + job)→ MediaConvert → S3 hls/ + RDS → Learner.
Playback flow: Learner → Cognito JWT → CloudFront → ALB → ECS (validate JWT, issue playback token, write AccessLog to DynamoDB) → Manifest + AES-128 key → Segments downloaded from S3 via 60-second presigned URLs → HLS Player → Dynamic Watermark.
AI branch: DynamoDB AccessLog → EventBridge Scheduler (every 5 minutes) → Lambda Anomaly Detection → Isolation Forest → If an anomaly is detected → SNS → Admin email.
General diagram: AWS Services Used AWS Lambda: Handle upload handling, license verification, JWT authorization, and AI anomaly detection logic. Amazon DynamoDB: On-demand NoSQL storage for sessions, DRM logs, and metadata. Amazon CloudWatch & AWS CloudTrail: Centralize audit trails and application logs. AWS KMS & AWS Secrets Manager: Secure cryptographic keys and API tokens. Amazon SNS: Broadcasts automated email alerts to administrators upon detecting anomalies. AWS EventBridge: Triggers the AI anomaly detection Lambda function every 5 minutes. Amazon ECS Fargate, Amazon ECR & Application Load Balancer: Run the Spring Boot backend (API, authentication, playback tokens, MeiaConvert transcoding) as a container without server administration. Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL: Stores course, chapter and lesson data. Amazon S3: Stores raw videos, encrypted HLS, the static frontend and the AI model. Amazon CloudFront, AWS WAF, Amazon Route 53 & AWS Certificate Manager: Deliver the frontend/API over HTTPS, protect the edge and manage the domain. Evaluation Against 6 AWS Well-Architected Pillars Pillar Implementation Design AWS / Cloudflare Services Used Security Least-privilege IAM roles, no static access keys; encryption at rest (SSE-KMS) & in transit (TLS); AES-128 encrypted HLS content; secrets in Secrets Manager; edge protection with AWS WAF; security-group chain allowing only CloudFront → ALB → ECS → RDS; Cognito group authorization in Spring Security. AWS IAM, KMS, Secrets Manager, WAF, Cognito, VPC Reliability ALB across 2 AZs with health checks; ECS restarts failed tasks; RDS automated backups for 7 days; S3 durability of 11 nines (99.999999999%). RDS can be upgraded to Multi-AZ and ECS to 2 tasks in production. Amazon ECS, ALB, RDS, S3 Operational Excellence Centralized logs with CloudWatch Logs and CloudTrail; automatic anomaly alerts through Amazon SNS; backend packaged as a Docker image in ECR and redeployed with a single ECS service update. Amazon CloudWatch, AWS CloudTrail, SNS, ECR Performance Efficiency Frontend cached at CloudFront edge locations; ECS Fargate scales by task count; video segments downloaded directly from S3 without passing through the backend; DynamoDB on-demand scales automatically. Amazon CloudFront, ECS Fargate, S3, DynamoDB Cost Optimization Pay-as-you-go; no DRM licensing and no paid transcoding service; no NAT Gateway; AWS Free Tier credits and always-free services (Lambda, DynamoDB, SNS, EventBridge); ECS/RDS turned off outside working hours. AWS Free Tier, ECS Fargate, Lambda, DynamoDB Sustainability Shared AWS managed infrastructure; Fargate provisions only the CPU/RAM needed; the AI Lambda runs only a few seconds every 5 minutes; lifecycle rules delete leftover raw videos. AWS Fargate, Lambda, S3 Lifecycle 4. Technical Implementation Implementation Scope:
In-Scope: Protection of AES-128 encrypted HLS video, JWT authentication through Cognito, short-lived playback tokens validated by the backend, segment delivery from private S3 via presigned URLs, access logging to DynamoDB, automatic AI log analysis with SNS alerts, dynamic watermarking. Out-of-Scope: Protection of PDF/Word documents, hardware DRM (HDCP) or commercial DRM (Widevine/PlayReady/FairPlay) integration, real-time livestream processing. Implementation Phases:
Week 1-3: Study Cognito, ECS Fargate, RDS, S3, KMS; design the AWS architecture; set up accounts, the VPC and the dev environment (Spring Boot, React, Docker). Week 4-6: Create the S3 bucket and the presigned-URL upload flow; write VideoProcessingService using MediaConvert for HLS transcoding + AES-128 encryption; build a basic React player with hls.js. Week 7-8: Build the playback-token API, manifest rewriting, key delivery and segment redirects; integrate Cognito (sign-up, OTP, sign-in, groups); package with Docker and deploy to ECS Fargate + ALB + RDS; configure CloudFront and AWS WAF. Week 9-10: Test the token lifecycle; write AccessLog to DynamoDB; train the Isolation Forest model (locally) and serialize it to a .pkl file on S3 (models/ prefix); write the Anomaly Detection Lambda; create a 5-minute EventBridge Scheduler; integrate CloudWatch + SNS; develop the dynamic watermark. Week 11: Integrate the dynamic watermark and device fingerprint into the video player; build the leak-tracing tool; internal security testing (pen-test, API authorization checks); cost optimization and AWS Budgets review. Week 12: Fix bugs, refine UI/UX, record demo video (5-7 mins), write technical blog, finalize workshop lab guide. 5. Timeline & Milestones Week 1-3: Architecture design, account setup, and theoretical research. Week 4-6: Media pipeline setup and automated video transcoding. Week 7-8: Access control, JWT authentication, and secure playback integration. Week 9-10: AI anomaly detection integration and token lifecycle testing. Week 11: Dynamic watermarking integration and security penetration testing. Week 12: Bug fixing, demo recording, documentation, and final presentation. 6. Budget Estimation Estimated total infrastructure cost is about ~$165 USD/month running 24/7 in the Singapore region (scenario: 100 hours of stored video + 100 hours watched/month). Running ECS and RDS only during working hours (~8 hours/day) brings it down to about ~$60–75 USD/month. Note: Actual costs vary based on usage, region, pricing plans, and AWS Free Tier eligibility.
Infrastructure Cost Breakdown:
Amazon ECS Fargate: ~$93 (1 task 2 vCPU / 4 GB + 50 GB ephemeral storage) Application Load Balancer: ~$23 (1 ALB, low traffic) Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL: ~$21 (db.t4g.micro Single-AZ + 20 GB gp3) Amazon Cognito: $0.00 (User Pool authentication) AWS WAF: ~$12 (1 Web ACL + 7 rules) AWS Route 53: ~$0.50 (1 hosted zone, domain registration not included) Amazon S3: ~$2 (~70 GB of HLS + frontend + model) AWS Secrets Manager: ~$0.40 (API tokens and credentials) Amazon CloudFront: $0.00 (Always Free 1 TB/month) AWS KMS: ~$1.15 (Customer Managed Key for secrets encryption) AWS Lambda: $0.00 (Covered by Free Tier for 50k invocations) Amazon API Gateway: ~$0.10 (20k REST API calls) Amazon DynamoDB: $0.00 (On-Demand Free Tier) Amazon CloudWatch & ECR: ~$0.75 (Audit logs and alarms) AWS EventBridge: $0.00 (Triggering anomaly detection every 5 mins) Resource Clean-up Plan:
AWS: elete the remaining resources (CloudFront, WAF, S3, ECR, Lambda, DynamoDB, SNS, EventBridge, Cognito, KMS, Secrets Manager, VPC, CloudWatch Log Groups, Route 53 records). Priority: Delete the ECS service/cluster, the ALB and RDS right after recording the demo, since they are billed hourly. 7. Risk Assessment Risk Matrix & Mitigation Strategies:
Long video transcoding exceeding timeouts (Medium impact, medium probability): The /upload/process API runs synchronously while CloudFront waits at most 60 seconds. Demo with short videos; the improvement is background processing (return 202 and poll the status). AWS lacks full native DRM (High impact, low probability): Clearly define scope around secure video access, anti-sharing, and traceability. Enable requireSignedURLs, short-lived tokens, and watermarks. MVP does not equal Widevine/PlayReady/FairPlay. Signed Token leakage or incorrect expiration (Medium impact, medium probability): Set short TTLs (1 hour), limit concurrent device sessions, and combine with AI anomaly detection. AI model false-positive predictions (Medium impact, medium probability): Start with Isolation Forest, tune contamination thresholds properly, and log false-positives for periodic retraining. Short internship duration (6 weeks) (High impact, low probability): Prioritize MVP first: Upload → Process → Authorization → Secure Playback, then integrate AI and watermarks. Cost overruns (Medium impact, low probability): Setup strict budget alerts on both AWS and Cloudflare. 8. Expected Outcomes Technical Improvements: Build an automated secure media pipeline (AES-128 HLS transcoding + encryption), apply a serverless container architecture on AWS and integrate automatic AI anomaly detection. Long-Term Value: Provide a cost-effective, highly scalable digital content protection framework that helps SME education platforms comprehensively protect their intellectual property.

title: AWS KMS & Secrets Manager
content:
Step 1: Create an AWS KMS Encryption Key Go to AWS KMS and select Create a new key.

title: Protecting the Admin Portal with AWS WAF
content:
AWS WAF replaces Cloudflare WAF and Cloudflare Zero Trust. The admin UI is the /{lang}/admin/* routes of the same React app, so what must be protected is the API: every admin action goes through /api/v1/admin/** and /api/v1/ai/**.
Step 1: Create an IP Set for Administrators Go to AWS WAF & Shield > IP sets > region Global (CloudFront) > Create IP set. Name: securelearn-admin-allowlist > IP version: IPv4. IP addresses: the admin machine’s public IP as /32 (e.g. 203.0.113.10/32) > Create IP set. Step 2: Create the Web ACL Web ACLs > Create web ACL > Resource type: Amazon CloudFront distributions > Name: securelearn-waf. Add AWS resources: select the SecureLearn distribution. Add managed rule groups: enable Core rule set, Known bad inputs, Amazon IP reputation list. Add my own rules > Rule builder: Name: admin-ip-allowlist > If a request: matches all the statements (AND). Statement 1: URI path > Starts with string > /api/v1/admin (create a similar rule for /api/v1/ai). Statement 2: Negate > Originates from an IP address in > securelearn-admin-allowlist. Action: Block > Add rule. Add my own rules > Rate-based rule: auth-rate-limit, limit 100 requests / 5 minutes / IP, Scope-down: URI path starts with /api/v1/auth/ (against password and OTP guessing), Action Block. Add my own rules > Rate-based rule: rate-limit-per-ip, limit 2000 requests / 5 minutes, Action Block. A learner watching a video generates about 50 segment requests every 5 minutes, so this threshold does not affect normal users. Rule priority: admin-ip-allowlist first > Default action: Allow > Create web ACL. Step 3: Test From an IP not in the allow-list, call https://learn.yourdomain.com/api/v1/admin/user > 403 from WAF. From the admin IP, the admin pages work normally. Call POST /api/v1/auth/login with a wrong password more than 100 times in 5 minutes > blocked. Step 4: Fix Authorization in the Backend WAF is only a temporary barrier. In the current code, SecurityConfiguration declares hasRole("ADMIN") for the pattern "/api/v1/admin", which does not match the sub-paths /register, /update, /delete, /user. As a result, any signed-in account can create and delete accounts and reset other users’ passwords. Fix the pattern to match all sub-paths, then rebuild the image and update the ECS service (section 5.3.3):
.requestMatchers("/api/v1/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN") .requestMatchers("/api/v1/ai/**").hasRole("ADMIN") After the fix, a learner token calling admin APIs gets a JSON 403 from ApiAccessDeniedHandler even from an allowed IP.
Do not enforce MFA on the user pool yet: AuthService.login does not handle the SOFTWARE_TOKEN_MFA challenge, so enabling it breaks sign-in.
Step 5: Monitor CloudTrail Go to CloudTrail > Event history to see management actions on AWS resources for the last 90 days (enabled by default, free). For longer retention, create a securelearn-trail trail that writes Management events to an S3 bucket.

content:
Summary Report: “The Invariable Lessons of Tech and Humanity: Key Takeaways from Amazon CTO Werner Vogels” Event Objectives “Navigating the Future of Cloud & AI in Vietnam” brought the technology community together with AWS and industry experts. Its themes included Cloud and AI trends, large-scale data architecture, operational excellence, and the skills software engineers need in the future. This report summarizes key insights shared by Dr. Werner Vogels, CTO & VP of Amazon.com.
The source document does not specify the event date or venue.
Speaker Dr. Werner Vogels – CTO & VP, Amazon.com Key Highlights Dynamo and choosing technology based on real needs The keynote described a database incident during a peak shopping period that caused a prolonged outage and significant losses. An analysis of query patterns showed that most of the workload consisted of Key-Value operations, while only a smaller portion required complex relational capabilities. The lesson is to understand how an application uses data before choosing its architecture; this analysis also contributed to the development of Dynamo and DynamoDB.
Four principles of operational excellence Measure at P99.9: Average latency can hide the experience of the most affected users. High-percentile measurements help identify and improve slow cases. Design assuming failures will happen: Distributed systems should continue operating when a component or an availability zone fails. Practice GameDays: Simulate failures to test detection, recovery, and failover. Understand the impact of usage-based pricing: With pay-as-you-go, cost and operational quality need continuous attention. The “Renaissance Developer” The speaker encouraged engineers to develop five qualities: curiosity and continuous learning; systems thinking; ownership; deep expertise combined with broad, T-shaped knowledge; and communication skills to understand business goals and explain technical trade-offs.
AI as an assistant, with people remaining accountable AI can accelerate prototyping and support software development, but its output still requires human review for correctness, security, edge cases, and performance. Judgment, creativity, empathy, and professional responsibility remain core engineering capabilities.
Key Takeaways Think from first principles: Analyze actual data patterns and access behavior before selecting a database or adopting a technology. Measure performance appropriately: Track P99.9 alongside averages to understand latency in the worst cases. Design for resilience: Expect failures and validate recovery through exercises such as GameDays. Build well-rounded capabilities: Combine deep technical expertise with systems thinking, communication, and business understanding. Use AI responsibly: Treat AI as a productivity tool and review generated code before production use. Applying to Work Identify an application’s main queries and read/write patterns before selecting a database. Track percentile latency and set performance objectives based on user experience. Plan failure, recovery, and failover tests for critical system components. Use AI to assist with prototyping and implementation while personally verifying security, logic, and performance. Develop systems thinking and explain technical decisions in terms stakeholders can understand. Event Experience The keynote connected practical operational lessons with system-design principles and career guidance for engineers. The Dynamo story illustrated the value of designing around actual usage patterns, while the discussion of AI emphasized that technology can assist work but does not replace human judgment and accountability.

title: AWS Elemental MediaConvert HLS Transcoding
content:
This optional exercise creates an AES-128-encrypted HLS output with AWS Elemental MediaConvert. Replace the placeholder values with values for your AWS account and SecureLearn lesson. The current SecureLearn upload and playback flow also stores generated lessons under hls/; keep an immutable key and the key delivery URL consistent with the player.
Important: The job below uses the MediaConvert AES-128 static key setting. Do not publish or expose the static key value in the application source, lesson metadata, or public S3 objects.
Prerequisites Complete section 5.4.1 and use the securelearn-media-<account-id> bucket. Run MediaConvert in the same AWS Region as the bucket (the workshop uses ap-southeast-1). Have the ARN of the SecureLearn-Key KMS key from section 5.3.4. Use a short test video stored under videos/<courseId>/. MediaConvert is billed for transcoding. Use a short test clip and review current AWS pricing before submitting a job.
Step 1: Create a MediaConvert service role In IAM > Roles, create a role for the AWS Elemental MediaConvert service. Name it securelearn-mediaconvert-role. In the role’s Permissions tab, choose Add permissions and attach the existing S3 and KMS permission policies available in your account. Make sure the attached S3 permissions allow the role to locate/list the bucket, read source objects under videos/, and write output objects under hls/. The KMS permissions and key policy must allow the role to use SecureLearn-Key for the SSE-KMS bucket. In the key policy for SecureLearn-Key, allow securelearn-mediaconvert-role to use the key. The role needs to decrypt the SSE-KMS source and use the key when writing SSE-KMS output. If the MediaConvert console creates a service role while you create the first job, use that role instead and attach the same existing S3 and KMS permission policies through Add permissions. Step 2: Start a MediaConvert job Open AWS Elemental MediaConvert in the Region where the S3 bucket was created. Choose Jobs > Create job. In Job settings, select securelearn-mediaconvert-role. Configure the input in the console: Set Input 1 > Input file to s3://<bucket>/videos/<courseId>/<timestamp>_<name>.mp4. Keep the video selector at its default. Under Audio selectors, use Audio Selector 1 with Default selection set to Default. Set Timecode source to Start at 0 (zero-based). Add an Apple HLS output group. Set its Destination to s3://<bucket>/hls/<courseId>/<timestamp>_<name>/master. Use a unique <timestamp>_<name> prefix for each job. In the HLS group settings, set Segment length to 6 seconds and Segment control to Segmented files. Set Minimum segment length to 0 if the field is shown. In the HLS encryption settings, enable encryption and choose AES-128 with Static key. Enter a randomly generated 16-byte key as 32 hexadecimal characters, set the key URL to securelearn-key, and include the initialization vector in the manifest. Do not reuse the key across lessons or expose it in public storage. The securelearn-key URL must be implemented or configured in SecureLearn as the endpoint that returns the matching static key; it must not reveal the key in the public manifest. Console labels can vary slightly by Region or UI version, but enter the values above in the corresponding input, HLS group, encryption, video, and audio settings.
Step 3: Run and monitor the job Choose Create to submit the job. In Jobs, wait until the status is COMPLETE. If it fails, open the job details and check the IAM or KMS access error before retrying. Open the destination prefix in Amazon S3 and confirm that the playlist and media segments were created.

title: AI Anomaly Detection & Alerting
content:
Update the SecureLearn Anomaly Detection Pipeline This step-by-step guide updates an existing SecureLearn AI monitoring deployment. It follows the supplied deployment guide: upload model v2, preserve the production AccessLog table, update the Lambda image and permissions, verify the stream and EventBridge triggers, then test alerts through the web application.
The pipeline uses:
Amazon S3 for the Isolation Forest model. Amazon ECR for the Lambda container image. AWS Lambda (securelearn-anomaly-detection) to score playback activity. DynamoDB Streams on AccessLog as the primary near-real-time trigger. EventBridge as a five-minute fallback trigger. DynamoDB AnomalyAlert and Amazon SNS for recorded alerts and email notifications. Amazon CloudWatch Logs for processing diagnostics. Use Region ap-southeast-1 (Singapore) for all resources.
Before you begin This is an update and verification procedure, not a clean deployment. It assumes the S3 model bucket, AccessLog and AnomalyAlert tables, Lambda function and execution role, ECR repository, and SNS topic already exist. The AccessLog index/stream mapping and EventBridge rule/target are verified or completed in the steps below. Do not recreate or delete the shared AccessLog table. If a foundational resource is missing, stop and complete the initial deployment procedure before continuing.
You need:
AWS CLI v2 configured with a profile that can update these resources. Docker Desktop running. The anomaly-lambda project folder containing handler.py, Dockerfile, requirements.txt, lambda-policy.json, lambda-env.json, and filter-criteria.json. isolation_forest_securelearn_v2.pkl in the project folder. This is the single-file, 12-feature model; do not pair it with the older scaler/model files. An authorized test account and a staging or workshop web application for end-to-end testing. Set LOG_TIMEZONE to UTC in lambda-env.json. The backend stores accessedTime in UTC without a timezone suffix.
Step 0: Configure PowerShell and AWS CLI Open PowerShell in the anomaly-lambda folder. Configure a named AWS CLI profile: aws configure --profile my-profile $env:AWS_PROFILE = "my-profile" $REGION = "ap-southeast-1" $ACCOUNT = aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text $REPO = "securelearn-anomaly" $IMAGE = "$ACCOUNT.dkr.ecr.$REGION.amazonaws.com/${REPO}:v4" $FUNC = "securelearn-anomaly-detection" $ROLE = "securelearn-anomaly-lambda-role" $BUCKET = "securelearn-models-$ACCOUNT" echo $ACCOUNT Confirm the output is your 12-digit AWS account ID. The profile and variables apply only to this PowerShell window; rerun this step if you open another one. Never put access keys in the guide or source files.
Step 1: Upload model v2 to S3 Upload the model to the existing model bucket and keep the key under models/:
aws s3 cp .\isolation_forest_securelearn_v2.pkl "s3://$BUCKET/models/isolation_forest_securelearn_v2.pkl" aws s3 ls "s3://$BUCKET/models/" Confirm the v2 .pkl object is listed. Do not change the video/HLS bucket or make the model bucket public. The Lambda execution role should read the model using IAM; do not add access keys to the function. Step 2: Verify the AccessLog index and stream AccessLog contains backend logs. Preserve its records and key schema. Confirm its existing indexes:
aws dynamodb describe-table --table-name AccessLog --region $REGION --query "Table.GlobalSecondaryIndexes[].{Name:IndexName,Status:IndexStatus}" The Lambda expects LogInADay (actionType + accessedTime) and byUserTime (userEmail + accessedTime). If byUserTime is missing, add only that index:
@' [{"Create":{"IndexName":"byUserTime","KeySchema":[{"AttributeName":"userEmail","KeyType":"HASH"},{"AttributeName":"accessedTime","KeyType":"RANGE"}],"Projection":{"ProjectionType":"ALL"}}}] '@ | Set-Content .\byusertime-gsi.json -Encoding ascii aws dynamodb update-table --table-name AccessLog --region $REGION ` --attribute-definitions AttributeName=userEmail,AttributeType=S AttributeName=accessedTime,AttributeType=S ` --global-secondary-index-updates file://byusertime-gsi.json Wait until byUserTime is ACTIVE before changing the stream. Check the current stream setting:
aws dynamodb describe-table --table-name AccessLog --region $REGION --query "Table.StreamSpecification" If streams are disabled, enable them with the NEW_IMAGE stream view type:
aws dynamodb update-table --table-name AccessLog --region $REGION ` --stream-specification StreamEnabled=true,StreamViewType=NEW_IMAGE If the stream is already enabled with NEW_IMAGE, do not update it. If it is enabled with another view type, coordinate the change and set it to NEW_IMAGE; DynamoDB may issue a new stream ARN, which you must retrieve in Step 5. Continue only after the index is active and the stream is enabled. Step 3: Update the Lambda role permissions Replace the account placeholder in the local policy and environment files:
foreach ($f in "lambda-policy.json", "lambda-env.json") { (Get-Content $f -Raw) -replace "ACCOUNT_ID", $ACCOUNT | Set-Content $f -NoNewline } Check that lambda-env.json points to the existing model bucket, models/isolation_forest_securelearn_v2.pkl, AccessLog, AnomalyAlert, both GSI names, the correct SNS topic ARN, and LOG_TIMEZONE UTC. Keep LOCK_ON_DETECT set to false until the dedicated lockout test in Step 9.
If either file contains an account ID from another environment instead of the ACCOUNT_ID placeholder, update those account-specific ARN and bucket values to the current account before applying the policy.
Update the existing Lambda execution role policy:
aws iam put-role-policy --role-name $ROLE --policy-name securelearn-anomaly-access ` --policy-document file://lambda-policy.json aws iam get-role --role-name $ROLE --query "Role.Arn" --output text The policy must allow only the required operations: read the model object in S3; query AccessLog and its two GSIs; read its DynamoDB stream; query and write AnomalyAlert; publish to the alert SNS topic; and, for the optional lockout feature, use the required Cognito actions scoped to the intended user pool. Keep the existing Lambda trust relationship and basic CloudWatch logging permission.
Step 4: Build and deploy the Lambda image Log in to ECR and build the container for Lambda’s x86_64 runtime:
aws ecr get-login-password --region $REGION | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin "$ACCOUNT.dkr.ecr.$REGION.amazonaws.com" docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64 --provenance=false --sbom=false -t $IMAGE --push . The --provenance=false and --sbom=false options keep the pushed image manifest compatible with Lambda. Use a new image tag instead of v4 if that tag is already being used for a different build.
Update the existing function code, wait for the update to finish, then update its complete environment from lambda-env.json:
aws lambda update-function-code --function-name $FUNC --image-uri $IMAGE --region $REGION aws lambda wait function-updated-v2 --function-name $FUNC --region $REGION aws lambda update-function-configuration --function-name $FUNC ` --environment file://lambda-env.json --region $REGION aws lambda wait function-updated-v2 --function-name $FUNC --region $REGION Do not use a partial environment update; it can remove variables the function still needs. Verify the image and model key:
aws lambda get-function --function-name $FUNC --region $REGION ` --query "{Image:Code.ImageUri,Status:Configuration.LastUpdateStatus,Environment:Configuration.Environment.Variables}" Confirm the update succeeded and the environment contains the v2 model key, correct table/index names, SNS topic ARN, and LOCK_ON_DETECT set to false. Step 5: Connect or verify the DynamoDB Stream trigger Get the current stream ARN:
$STREAM_ARN = aws dynamodb describe-table --table-name AccessLog ` --query "Table.LatestStreamArn" --output text --region $REGION echo $STREAM_ARN Check existing event source mappings before creating one:
aws lambda list-event-source-mappings --function-name $FUNC --region $REGION ` --query "EventSourceMappings[].{UUID:UUID,State:State,Source:EventSourceArn}" If an enabled mapping already points to this stream, keep it and do not create a duplicate. Otherwise create the mapping:
aws lambda create-event-source-mapping --function-name $FUNC ` --event-source-arn $STREAM_ARN ` --starting-position LATEST ` --batch-size 100 ` --maximum-batching-window-in-seconds 30 ` --maximum-retry-attempts 2 ` --maximum-record-age-in-seconds 3600 ` --filter-criteria file://filter-criteria.json ` --region $REGION The filter file should pass only playback INSERT events with PLAYBACK, MANIFEST_REQUEST, KEY_REQUEST, or SEGMENT_REQUEST action types. Wait for the mapping state to become Enabled. Because the stream uses LATEST, new records trigger the function; old records are not replayed. Step 6: Confirm the SNS email subscription The Lambda environment must reference the existing securelearn-anomaly-alerts topic in this Region. Check its subscriptions before adding another:
$TOPIC = "arn:aws:sns:${REGION}:${ACCOUNT}:securelearn-anomaly-alerts" aws sns list-subscriptions-by-topic --topic-arn $TOPIC --region $REGION If the intended administrator email is not already subscribed, add it:
aws sns subscribe --topic-arn $TOPIC --protocol email ` --notification-endpoint "admin@example.com" --region $REGION Replace the example with an authorized monitoring address. Open the confirmation email and confirm the subscription; SNS will not deliver alert emails until it is confirmed. If the topic does not exist, stop and create it using the initial deployment procedure. Then set its ARN in lambda-env.json and update the Lambda environment again using the full-file commands from Step 4. Step 7: Verify the EventBridge fallback The scheduled rule should invoke the same Lambda every five minutes. Check the existing rule and target. If the rule is missing, list-targets-by-rule can return ResourceNotFoundException; continue with the put-rule command below:
aws events list-targets-by-rule --rule securelearn-anomaly-every-5min --region $REGION Create or update the named schedule and obtain its ARN. put-rule with this same name updates the existing schedule rather than creating a duplicate:
$RULE_ARN = aws events put-rule --name securelearn-anomaly-every-5min ` --schedule-expression "rate(5 minutes)" --region $REGION --query RuleArn --output text $FUNC_ARN = aws lambda get-function --function-name $FUNC --region $REGION ` --query Configuration.FunctionArn --output text aws events put-targets --rule securelearn-anomaly-every-5min ` --targets "Id=1,Arn=$FUNC_ARN" --region $REGION The target ID is stable, so this command creates or updates the target. Ensure the Lambda resource policy allows EventBridge to invoke the function. Add the permission only if the eventbridge-5min statement does not already exist:
aws lambda add-permission --function-name $FUNC --statement-id eventbridge-5min ` --action lambda:InvokeFunction --principal events.amazonaws.com ` --source-arn $RULE_ARN --region $REGION The five-minute fallback complements the stream; it does not replace it.
Step 8: Test detection through the web application Use the staging or workshop application and an authorized test account. Do not use real student accounts or run a crawler against a production service.
Watch a video normally for three to five minutes and confirm the backend writes playback records to AccessLog. Review Lambda diagnostics:
aws logs tail /aws/lambda/$FUNC --since 10m --region $REGION If the workshop provides an approved crawler test, run it only against the test environment with a dedicated test account. Confirm the test result in CloudWatch Logs, the AnomalyAlert table, and the confirmed SNS email subscription. A new alert should have status = OPEN; detection scores depend on the input data and model configuration.
Do not use seed_test_logs.py or insert synthetic data into the shared production AccessLog table as part of this procedure. Step 9: Test Cognito account lockout safely (optional) Lockout is disabled by default. It can sign a user out and disable that Cognito account Generate the approved test pattern using only the disposable account. Verify the AnomalyAlert record and that Cognito shows the test user as disabled. Then immediately: Set LOCK_ON_DETECT back to "false" in lambda-env.json. Update the Lambda environment with the full file and wait for the update to complete. Fewamok844@anomart.com using tool to download illegally so it was locked Re-enable the disposable user in Amazon Cognito > User pools > the user pool > Users > select the user > Actions > Enable user access.

title: Workshop
content:
SecureLearn: A Digital Content Protection System for Educational Platforms In this workshop, you will build SecureLearn, a cost-effective video content protection solution designed for small and medium-sized educational centers (SMEs). The whole system run on AWS:
A Spring Boot backend runs on ECS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer. It handles authentication through Cognito, issues playback tokens, and transcodes + encrypts AES-128 HLS with FFmpeg. Data lives in RDS for PostgreSQL, DynamoDB and S3. The ReactJS frontend is delivered through CloudFront, protected by AWS WAF. An AI anomaly detection system runs on Lambda (container image on ECR), triggered by a DynamoDB Stream and EventBridge. Workshop Content Workshop Overview Prerequisites Deploying the Control Plane on AWS Amazon Cognito User Pool AI Anomaly Detection Lambda Spring Boot Backend on ECS AWS KMS & Secrets Manager SNS & EventBridge Alerts Deploying the AWS-Media-Plane S3 storage CloudFront WAF AWS Elemental MediaConvert AI Monitoring & Alerting System Clean Up

title: Clean Up Resources
content:
After completing the workshop and recording your demonstration, clean up all provisioned resources to avoid unexpected charges.
1. Clean Up AWS Resources AWS WAF & CloudFront (us-east-1 / Global): Disassociate and delete the Web ACL securelearn-waf and the IP set securelearn-admin-allowlist; disable and then delete the distribution, and remove the CloudFront Function securelearn-spa-rewrite. Amazon ECS & ECR: Set the desired count for securelearn-backend-svc to 0, delete the service and the cluster securelearn-cluster, deregister the task definition securelearn-backend, and delete the securelearn-backend repository. Elastic Load Balancing & ACM: Delete the ALB securelearn-alb and the target group securelearn-backend-tg, then delete the ACM certificates in both ap-southeast-1 (for the ALB) and us-east-1 (for CloudFront). Amazon RDS: Delete the database securelearn-db (deselect the final snapshot option if you do not need to retain the data) and the subnet group securelearn-db-subnets. Amazon DynamoDB: Delete AnomalyAlert; delete the AccessLog table only after the backend has been shut down and the data is no longer needed. Amazon S3: Empty and delete the buckets securelearn-media-<account-id>, securelearn-web-<account-id>, and securelearn-models-<account-id>. AWS Secrets Manager & KMS: Delete the secret securelearn/backend and schedule the deletion of the KMS key SecureLearn-Key (with a minimum waiting period of 7 days)—perform this only after the video bucket has been deleted. Amazon Cognito: Delete the User Pool SecureLearn. Route 53: Delete the learn and origin records, as well as any ACM validation records. Amazon VPC: Delete the VPC securelearn-vpc (including its subnets, security groups, and S3 Gateway endpoint). AWS Lambda, EventBridge, SNS & ECR: Delete the Lambda event-source mapping and function, the securelearn-anomaly-every-5min EventBridge rule and its target, the securelearn-anomaly-alerts SNS topic, and the securelearn-anomaly ECR repository. IAM: Delete the roles securelearn-ecs-execution-role, securelearn-ecs-task-role, and securelearn-anomaly-lambda-role. Amazon CloudWatch & CloudTrail: Manually delete any remaining ECS and Lambda log groups; delete the trail securelearn-trail if it was created. aws events remove-targets --rule securelearn-anomaly-every-5min --ids 1 --region $REGION aws events delete-rule --name securelearn-anomaly-every-5min --region $REGION $ESM = aws lambda list-event-source-mappings --function-name $FUNC --region $REGION --query "EventSourceMappings[0].UUID" --output text aws lambda delete-event-source-mapping --uuid $ESM --region $REGION aws lambda delete-function --function-name $FUNC --region $REGION aws ecr delete-repository --repository-name $REPO --force --region $REGION aws iam delete-role-policy --role-name $ROLE --policy-name securelearn-anomaly-access aws iam detach-role-policy --role-name $ROLE --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole aws iam delete-role --role-name $ROLE $TOPIC = aws sns list-topics --region $REGION --query "Topics[?ends_with(TopicArn, ':securelearn-anomaly-alerts')].TopicArn" --output text aws sns delete-topic --topic-arn $TOPIC --region $REGION aws s3 rb "s3://$BUCKET" --force aws dynamodb delete-table --table-name AnomalyAlert --region $REGION aws logs delete-log-group --log-group-name /aws/lambda/$FUNC --region $REGION The above commands delete: EventBridge rule securelearn-anomaly-every-5min, stream connection, Lambda securelearn-anomaly-detection, ECR repository securelearn-anomaly, role securelearn-anomaly-lambda-role, SNS topic securelearn-anomaly-alerts, bucket securelearn-models-, table AnomalyAlert and log group of Lambda. The AccessLog table is shared with the backend.
